claim: A learned stop/continue decision can be trained on a small model with counterfactual pairs (stop-right prefix vs minimally edited stop-wrong prefix) plus a written reason; CaRT beats base and plain SFT on interactive diagnosis (Qwen2.5-3B) and AIME 2025 (Qwen3-1.7B) at fewer tokens. One group, one paper; exact values are in figures only.
agent_test: Train or prompt a stop judge on counterfactual pairs from our own traces; compare stop quality vs fixed budget at equal mean tokens.

claim: Counterfactual (hard-negative) data is the most important ingredient of CaRT; reasons add a smaller consistent gain. Plain SFT learns a length heuristic (stop more as the chat grows). Without counterfactuals Qwen3-1.7B did worse than the fixed budget.
agent_test: Ablate: stop judge trained with and without hard negatives; check whether stop rate tracks turn count rather than information.

claim: Learned stoppers weaken under domain shift: on out-of-distribution dermatology, base and SFT models were worse than a naive fixed-count stop; CaRT stayed above it with a smaller margin. Probes lose gain out of distribution (thought calibration: up to 60% fewer tokens in-distribution, up to 20% OOD). Gap search: ESTAR transferred a stop classifier trained on USMLE and deepscaleR to GPQA with 98.9-100% accuracy retained over 6 models, so the OOD collapse looks specific to CaRT's small-model, one-shift setting rather than general; a feature-based decider also transferred with only calibration (d17).
agent_test: Fit the stop rule on one task family, test on another at equal tokens; report margin over fixed budget.
audit_note: ESTAR GPQA retention table is garbled in extraction (values seen 98.9-100.2%, one row 98.4%); the cross-method inference that the OOD drop is specific to CaRT is the researcher's hedged interpretation, not from the sources.

claim: Reasoning models often reach their final answer well before they stop: first round correct in over 92% of cases on easy sets (Chen), final answer reached after about 60% of steps on math (Liu and Wang). Redundant continuation is common.
agent_test: Log the earliest step at which our agent's answer equals its final answer; report the wasted-token share.
audit_note: Chen's >92% is the paper's aggregate statement; its figure shows some set-model bars near 89-90%.

claim: Training-free answer-based early exit saves large token shares with equal or slightly higher accuracy: DEER cuts CoT 19.1-80.1% with +0.3 to +5.0 accuracy over 11 models; Answer Consistency cuts over 40% of tokens on NQ; EAT 12-22% with no accuracy harm. A probe-based method that needs training (LYNX) reaches 35-70% fewer tokens with matched or better accuracy.
agent_test: Implement a trial-answer-and-confidence stop at 'Wait'-type transitions; compare to fixed budget at equal mean tokens.
audit_note: LYNX trains a hidden-state probe with conformal calibration, so it is not training-free; the sources do not call it training-free or answer-based. DEER, Answer Consistency and EAT numbers match.
claim_before_audit: Training-free answer-based early exit saves large token shares with equal or slightly higher accuracy: DEER cuts CoT 19.1-80.1% with +0.3 to +5.0 accuracy over 11 models; Answer Convergence over 40% on NQ; LYNX 35-70%; EAT 12-22%.

claim: Hidden-state probes predict whether an intermediate answer is correct (ROC-AUC above 0.7, ECE below 0.1 in distribution); as a stop rule they save about 24% tokens with no accuracy loss, but degrade on short-CoT models and out of distribution. Needs open weights.
agent_test: Not testable on a closed API agent; test a text-only analogue (self-rated sufficiency) if weights are unavailable.
audit_note: Zhang et al. abstract stresses probes generalize to some OOD sets; the degradation OOD is in their section 4.3 (math to knowledge domain) and in thought calibration (60% to 20%).

claim: Sample-level stopping for self-consistency works: Adaptive-Consistency cuts samples up to 7.9x with under 0.1% average accuracy loss; ESC cuts 33.8% (MATH) to 84.2% (Coin Flip) with similar accuracy; both beat fixed-budget SC at equal average samples.
agent_test: Replace fixed N-vote with a window or Bayesian stop; compare accuracy at equal mean samples.

claim: Parallel-trace pruning by confidence or length cuts tokens without loss: DeepConf up to 84.7% fewer tokens (AIME 2025, GPT-OSS-120B; 99.9% at @512 offline); short-m@k up to 40% fewer thinking tokens.
agent_test: Stop low-confidence or long traces early in a multi-trace run; equal-token comparison with majority vote.

claim: Shorter chains within the same question are more often correct than longer ones (up to 34.5% above the longest). Rival explanations: redundancy, or long chains reflect failed search. This is correlation; it does not prove that cutting causes success.
agent_test: Truncate chains at random points and at confidence points; test whether truncation or selection explains the gain.

claim: The opposite error exists: underthinking. Wrong answers use 225% more tokens with 418% more thought switches; a switching penalty raised accuracy on hard sets. A stop rule must not cut a promising line early.
agent_test: Count premature stops on hard items (answer would have improved) as a separate error rate.

claim: Confidence-based exit has false-positive risk: spurious confidence silences the model before self-correction (path-deviation paper); plain confidence averaging does not fix false positives (DEER failure analysis); confident-wrong traces exist (DeepConf). No paper quantifies the false-stop rate cleanly. Gap search: Sequential-EDFL reports premature-stop 0.083-0.092 at delta 0.1 and 13.2-22.7% sufficient-looking but wrong answers; ESTAR's threshold sweep shows tau .99 to .80 costs 3.8 accuracy points. Still no false-stop rate split by difficulty.
agent_test: Report false-stop rate next to token savings.
audit_note: Minor: DEER's appendix says averaging reduces false-positive probability but does not remove its dependence on noise, so 'does not fix' is slightly loose.

claim: Adaptive mode choice (think vs no-think) by difficulty helps: AdaptThink cuts length 53% and raises accuracy 2.4% on three math sets (R1-Distill-1.5B). But NoThinking is harmful on hard items (Qwen3-14B AIME 26.7 vs 70.0).
agent_test: Route easy items to a one-shot path at S0; measure accuracy by difficulty bin at equal tokens.

claim: Question-asking agents need a stop-asking rule: plain prompting to ask makes models worse than answering from initial info (MediQ); an abstention module gives +22.3% over basic interactive and +12.1% over non-interactive, still 10.3% below full info. QuestBench: models identify the right clarification question with over 80% accuracy on math tasks but only 40-50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q, and struggle to pick the right question even when they can solve the fully specified problem.
agent_test: Add a sufficiency check before answering; compare ask-then-answer vs answer-now at equal tokens.
audit_note: MediQ numbers match, but QuestBench's 80-90% vs 40-50% are question-selection accuracies on math (GSM-Q/GSME-Q) versus Logic-Q/Planning-Q, not solving versus finding the missing variable.
claim_before_audit: Question-asking agents need a stop-asking rule: plain prompting to ask makes models worse than answering from initial info (MediQ); an abstention module gives +22.3% over basic interactive and +12.1% over non-interactive, still 10.3% below full info. QuestBench: models solve but cannot find the missing variable (80-90% vs 40-50%).

claim: Context sufficiency is a separate skill from answering: large models (Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) answer well when context is sufficient but often answer wrongly instead of abstaining when it is not, while smaller models (Mistral 3, Gemma 2) hallucinate or abstain often even with sufficient context; sufficiency-guided selective generation raises the fraction of correct answers among those answered by 2-10% for Gemini, GPT and Gemma.
agent_test: Score an S0 sufficiency check separately; measure abstain vs wrong-answer rate.
audit_note: Abstract says selective generation improves the correct fraction among answered by 2-10% (en dash), not 210%; the second listed source (MediQ) does not address context sufficiency.
claim_before_audit: Context sufficiency is a separate skill from answering: large models answer well when context is sufficient but answer wrongly instead of abstaining when it is not; sufficiency-guided selective generation raises the correct fraction among answered (abstract: up to 210%).

claim: Longer thinking can reduce accuracy (inverse scaling; variance explanation), so more compute is not monotone; this supports a stop rule over a large fixed budget. Seen in abstracts only.
agent_test: Sweep thinking budget on our tasks; find the accuracy peak and whether a stop rule finds it.

claim: No independent replication or failed replication of CaRT was found by any searcher. Related early-exit ideas agree in direction but use different setups and no shared benchmark.
agent_test: Replicate CaRT's design on a second domain and base model.

claim: CaRT's own binary-reward RL on top of SFT made conversations longer with no math gain. Other reward designs did work in math: S-GRPO (correct-only, decaying with exit point; length -35.4 to -61.1%, accuracy +0.72 to +6.08), JET (truncated rollouts plus quality-gated length reward; Olympiad +4.6% at -46.3% length), ESTAR (stop-earliness reward; length x2.0-x7.5 at 95-100% accuracy). Steep exponential length penalties cause premature truncation on hard items (JET).
agent_test: Avoid RL; compare an SFT-style or prompted judge only.

claim: Classical stopping theory (Wald SPRT, Chow-Robbins) gives the form: stop when expected gain of one more step falls below its cost. CaRT's discounted objective has the same form. Not opened this session. Gap search: Hammar et al. (CDC 2026) derive stopping policies of this form for generate-verify-refine loops and report better cost-efficiency than prior stopping policies on a coding benchmark (abstract only); BEACON and the Pandora's Box paper use the same gain-vs-cost rule for sampling.
agent_test: Implement an explicit value-of-continuing estimate (chance the answer changes times expected gain vs token cost).

claim: A stop rule outside the model works where the model's own judgment does not: tool-using agents label failing sources useless 97-100% of the time yet rarely stop; a harness rule forcing an answer after 5 useless results lifts success (Qwen3-32B .509 to .572, Haiku 4.5 .501 to .598, Sonnet 5 .632 to .653 not significant) and replicated on 300 fresh questions. A stated step budget becomes a quota: doubling it doubles tool calls with no gain.
agent_test: Add an enforced integration step to the scaffold: after k consecutive no-gain steps force an answer. Never state the budget as a target.

claim: Text-only stop signals can match their cost: embedding convergence of consecutive drafts saves 38% tokens at quality parity versus a fixed iteration cap, while a per-round LLM judge erases the savings; screened LLM judges rank refinement rounds like experts (rho 0.58-0.90) but over-score by 1.4-2.3 points. No paper compares a prompted judge with a hidden-state probe head to head.
agent_test: Use cheap answer-stability checks every step and call a judge only on disagreement; screen the judge against labelled cases.

claim: Information sufficiency is not correctness: a stop rule with a guaranteed premature-stop bound (about 8-9%) still leaves 13.2-22.7% sufficient-looking but wrong outputs; a correctness gate cuts this to 10.9% (from 18.5%) at 12% to 16% overhead.
agent_test: Pair the stop judge with an independent check before commit; log high-confidence-wrong cases as the false-stop measure.

claim: Stopping and voting can be stacked: Pandora's Box UCB stop beats fixed best-of-N at equal average compute (win rate above 54%, 15-35% fewer samples); BEACON up to 80% fewer samples; PeerConf and MARS report further savings over DeepConf (second-hand, unopened). No opened paper tests trace-stop and vote-stop jointly at a strictly equal token budget.
agent_test: Test on our own set: per-trace stop only, vote stop only, both, at the same mean tokens.

claim: Nothing was found on LLMs versus humans on classic optimal-stopping tasks (secretary problem, costly sampling): zero arXiv hits and no web-search hit. LLM stopping work is limited to theory and inference-time sampling.
agent_test: If needed, run a small secretary and sampling-cost test with several models and compare with the 1/e rule.

claim: Stability-based and sufficiency-based stops are different events: commitment-boundary exit (answer logits) allows up to 55% shorter CoT; ESTAR and JET learn a sufficiency signal. No paper measures where the two disagree in interactive tasks. Joint learning of what to ask and when to stop is stated as future work by CaRT's authors and has no tested evidence beyond UoT and MediQ.
agent_test: Log both signals per step in our traces and count the disagreements before choosing one.
